variants.name: Per-instance std::sync::OnceLock cell
variants.implementation_notes: std ships the guard, not the lazy object: store a OnceLock in the entity and load through get_or_init, so the closure runs once even under concurrent access and get() answers 'was it loaded?' without forcing a load. Because the std cell has no stable fallible initializer, a store read that can fail caches Result<T, E> (the error is cached beside the value) or uses once_cell's get_or_try_init; a panic during initialization leaves the cell empty so the next access retries. LazyLock (1.80) is the deref-shaped sibling for process-wide values, and before 1.70 the once_cell crate provided both types.
pitfalls: A fallible loader must cache Result (std's get_or_try_init is not stable), which caches the error permanently; use once_cell for retry-after-error or add an explicit invalidate/refresh path.
get_or_init must not re-enter the same cell - the documented outcome is unspecified and currently deadlocks - and OnceLock is only Sync when the value is Send + Sync.
The cell makes the holder neither Copy nor Clone, so sharing the loaded value across threads constrains both the value and the containing entity.

variants.name: Static LazyLock for process-wide reference data
variants.implementation_notes: LazyLock is the deref-shaped sibling: 'static RATES: LazyLock<HashMap<Currency, Rate>> = LazyLock::new(load_rates);' initializes on the first dereference and every later use looks like a reference, the cleanest shape for process-wide immutable data loaded from the store. It blocks any dereferencing thread while another thread initializes, cannot take extra inputs after new(), and poisons permanently if the initializer panics - so it serves shared reference tables, not per-entity rows.
variants.code_sketch:
static RATES: LazyLock<HashMap<Currency, Decimal>> = LazyLock::new(load_rates);

fn rate(c: Currency) -> Decimal { RATES[&c] }
pitfalls: One instance per process: LazyLock cannot serve per-entity deferred rows (use a per-instance OnceLock), and the loaded data is never refreshed.
A panicking initializer poisons the static so every later access panics, and statics are never dropped - resources held by the loaded value are not released at exit.
